blocks.text: Jerusalem was both a royal center and a center of worship, bringing kingship, temple life, pilgrimage, judgment, and hopes for restored worship together in one place. This background clarifies why the psalm can move naturally from the house of Jehovah and the gathering tribes to the thrones of David and prayers for the city’s peace.

Jerusalem’s history extended from a Jebusite city to the Davidic capital and temple center, and later made the city a focal point of exile, return, and expectation. The psalm’s references to David’s house and the house of Jehovah therefore name two defining features of Jerusalem’s historical identity.

Because Jerusalem joined worship, pilgrimage, Davidic rule, judgment, and hopes for restoration, seeking its peace meant more than wishing for quiet streets. Within the psalm, the city’s good embraces the worshiping community, its shared life, and the house of Jehovah at its center.

One disputed reading places this song within a broader movement in the Psalms: communal songs remember sanctuary destruction and Babylonian exile, while Book V gathers thanksgiving for return, festival praise, Torah meditation, and Songs of Ascents directed toward worship. On that reading, Psalm 122’s glad journey to Jerusalem participates in a larger collection concerned with restored communal worship.
